Issued at 416 AM CDT Wed Sep 23 2026

A shortwave trough will eject off the Northern Rockies this 
morning, reaching the western Dakotas by the end of the day. 
Ahead of the shortwave, strong southerly return flow between a 
lee trough over central Montana and broad high pressure 
stretching from the Great Lakes to New England and the Canadian 
maritime provinces has maintained breezy conditions, widespread 
stratus clouds, and mild temperatures in the 50s over western 
and central North Dakota early this morning. The approaching 
shortwave, which is projected to be collocated with the left 
exit region of an upper level jet streak, is forecast to bring 
areas of showers across the state during the day today, with the
highest chances in the southwest this morning and northwest and
central during the afternoon. There could also be some lighter 
showers from the James River Valley to the Turtle Mountains this
morning on account of warm air advection induced by the low 
level jet. Low stratus is forecast to keep the boundary layer 
stable over central North Dakota this afternoon, but an EML 
above the boundary layer could yield enough buoyancy for some 
embedded thunderstorms to develop. These storms are unlikely to 
be strong, but there is a scenario back to the west that will 
need to be monitored later today. Some CAMs, most notably the 
HRRR with high run-to-run consistency, initiate storms along the
lee trough in west central and southwest North Dakota late this
afternoon. This timing and placement is now projected to be 
concurrent with the arrival of the mid/upper level trough axis, 
which lends increased confidence in both development and 
maintenance of widely scattered thunderstorms. Clusters of UH 
tracks indicative of strong to severe convection have been 
common in HRRR guidance, with CAPE around 1000 J/kg and deep 
layer shear around 30 kts. One of the key factors likely to 
regulate whether strong to severe storms are able to develop is
the erosion of cloud cover, which will be necessary to allow 
diurnal heating to sufficiently erode CIN. Because of this 
uncertainty and environmental parameters being barely 
supportive of severe convection, we will message a potential 
for strong thunderstorms during the late afternoon and evening, 
west and south of the Missouri River. Intensity of any evening 
storms should diminish by midnight, but showers and weaker 
thunderstorms may continue to propagate east/northeastward 
through central North Dakota late tonight. Aside from shower 
and thunderstorm chances, forecast highlights for today include
a mostly cloudy sky and breezy south-southeast winds around 
15-25 mph. Both wind and cloud cover could decrease in southwest
North Dakota this afternoon, where high temperatures could 
reach the lower 70s. Elsewhere, highs are likely to be limited 
to the lower and mid 60s.

An upper level ridge is forecast to develop over the region on 
Thursday, with the strong surface isobaric gradient shifting 
eastward. Decreasing clouds through the day should allow high 
temperatures to reach the lower 70s east to around 80 far west. 
On Friday, the upper ridge is forecast to shift eastward as a 
potent trough lands on the Pacific Northwest, all while a 
shortwave lifts off the Central Rockies toward the Northern 
Plains. Latest model guidance has slowed the shortwave, but NBM 
PoPs have significantly increased to around 60 to 80 percent in 
the eastern half of the state, temporally increasing from Friday
afternoon through Friday night before diminishing Saturday 
morning. Preceding cloud cover and southeasterly surface flow 
will likely bring high temperatures back into the 60s in south 
central North Dakota on Friday, but there is still a chance for 
lower to mid 70s across the west and north. As the late Friday 
shortwave departs, the Pacific Northwest trough is forecast to 
open and spin an occluding cyclone into Alberta and Saskatchewan
on Saturday. The southward extending cold/occluded front is 
forecast to move across the state Saturday afternoon and 
evening, with some timing uncertainty. This keeps the high 
temperature forecast less certain on Saturday, but the NBM has 
been consistently advertising lower to mid 70s in its 50th 
percentile output.

The main feature of interest heading into early next week is a 
deep but progressive trough moving from the Pacific Coast late 
Sunday into the Plains by mid week. Ensembles are in good 
agreement on the existence of the trough, but uncertainty in 
timing and placement of its strongest energy is evident. 
Cluster analysis reveals two distinct and nearly-equal outcomes 
in the evolution of the trough: one keeps the base of the trough
over the Desert Southwest for a longer period of time, allowing
a northern stream wave to deepen; the other is more progressive
and keeps the base of the trough north of the Deep South. Then
